sourceReview: Read bundled BSB Psalm 47 in full with each verse's related passages before drafting. References are thematic or literary comparisons, not an invented historical occasion. Scripture is never stored in the notes; it loads from the bundled BSB.

study.title: God is King of all the earth.
study.intro: Nine verses call every people to clap and shout for God, celebrate His ascent with trumpet blasts, and picture the nobles of the nations gathered as the people of Abraham's God.
study.context: The heading calls this a Psalm of the sons of Korah. It is an enthronement psalm, like Psalms 93 and 95–99, celebrating God as King. Verses 1–4 call all peoples to applaud and recall God choosing Israel's inheritance; verses 5–9 picture God 'ascending' with shouts and the ram's horn, perhaps recalling the ark being carried up to Zion (2 Samuel 6:15), and end with the nations' nobles gathered as 'the people of the God of Abraham' (verse 9), echoing the promise that all nations would be blessed through Abraham (Genesis 12:3). Church tradition has read verse 5 at the feast of the Ascension. The language of nations 'under our feet' in verse 3 is read within that wider hope for the nations. The Scripture is loaded unchanged from the bundled BSB, including the heading.
study.peopleNote: The heading credits this enthronement song to the sons of Korah, the Levite temple singers. Jacob is named in verse 4, where 'the pride of Jacob' means the land God gave his descendants. Abraham is named in verse 9; the app has no Abraham profile, so he is mentioned here without a link. Planned paintings show crowds, horns, thrones and landscapes; God is never portrayed as a human body.

verses.title: Clap your hands
verses.heading: A call to all peoples
verses.meaning: The heading names the sons of Korah. The psalm bursts open with a command to all peoples, not just Israel, to clap their hands and shout to God with triumph. Clapping was a way of acclaiming a king (2 Kings 11:12). The scope is global from the first line. This is a psalm of loud, joyful worship. It invites the whole world to celebrate God's kingship.
verses.context: 2 Kings 11:12 records the people clapping their hands and shouting 'Long live the king!' at Joash's coronation, and Isaiah 55:12 pictures the trees of the field clapping their hands. Psalm 47:1 invites every people to do the same for God.
explore: All you peoples
The invitation is universal. No nation is excluded from praising God.
A voice of triumph
The shout is loud and joyful. It celebrates a victorious King.
verses.reflect: When did you last praise God with real joy? What might help you do so today?
verses.alt: Many hands of different peoples clap together in sunlight.

verses.title: Great King over all
verses.heading: The LORD Most High
verses.meaning: How awesome is the LORD Most High, the great King over all the earth! The reason for the shout is given. God is awesome, worthy of reverent fear. He is the Most High, above every power. He is the great King, a title Assyrian emperors used of themselves. The psalm claims that title for the LORD alone. His rule extends over all the earth.
verses.context: Assyrian kings called themselves 'the great king' (2 Kings 18:19), and Malachi 1:14 says, 'I am a great King.' Psalm 47:2 gives that title to the LORD.
explore: Awesome
God inspires reverent fear. His greatness is overwhelming.
Over all the earth
God's rule has no borders. Every land is under Him.
verses.reflect: How does knowing God as the great King over all the earth change how you see world events?
verses.alt: A mountain range stretches beneath a vast dome of sky.

verses.title: Nations beneath us
verses.heading: God's victories for His people
verses.meaning: He subdues nations beneath us, and peoples under our feet. The psalm recalls God giving Israel victory over the nations, especially in the conquest of Canaan. The language is the standard idiom of ancient victory. Within this psalm, though, the nations who are subdued in verse 3 are invited to worship in verse 1 and gathered as God's people in verse 9. The notes read it within that wider hope, not as a claim of superiority over any modern people.
verses.context: Psalm 18:47 says God subdues peoples under me, but Psalm 47:9 sees the nations gathered as the people of Abraham's God. Isaiah 2:2–4 pictures nations streaming to Zion.
explore: Beneath us
The image is victory. It describes Israel's past conquest.
Peoples under our feet
Standard ancient language. The psalm's end transforms it.
verses.reflect: How does the psalm's hope for the nations shape how you see people of other backgrounds?
verses.alt: A stone footstool carved with distant lands sits before a throne.

verses.title: The pride of Jacob
verses.heading: An inheritance chosen in love
verses.meaning: He chooses our inheritance for us, the pride of Jacob, whom He loves. Selah. God chose the land for Israel. 'The pride of Jacob' refers to the land itself, Jacob's glory. The key phrase is 'whom He loves.' The inheritance comes from God's love, not Israel's merit. Selah pauses the first stanza. The verse grounds the people's celebration in being chosen and loved.
verses.context: Deuteronomy 7:7–8 says God chose Israel not because they were many but because He loved them, and Malachi 1:2 says, 'I have loved Jacob.' Psalm 47:4 calls the land the pride of Jacob.
explore: Our inheritance
The land is a gift. God Himself chose it for His people rather than letting them grab it.
Whom He loves
Love is the reason. The inheritance flows from God's affection.
verses.reflect: What inheritance has God given you out of love? How could you thank Him for it?
verses.alt: Green terraced hills with olive groves stretch under soft light.

verses.title: God has ascended
verses.heading: Shouts and the sound of the horn
verses.meaning: God has ascended amid shouts of joy, the LORD with the sound of the horn. The image is of a king going up to his throne in a procession. It probably recalls the ark being carried up to Jerusalem with shouting and trumpets (2 Samuel 6:15). The ark was the symbol of God's throne. Christians have long read this verse at the Ascension of Christ. The verse pictures a joyful coronation procession.
verses.context: 2 Samuel 6:15 describes David and Israel bringing up the ark with shouts and the sound of the horn, and Psalm 68:18 says, 'You have ascended on high.' Ephesians 4:8 applies Psalm 68 to Christ.
explore: Ascended
God goes up to His throne. The image is a coronation.
Sound of the horn
The ram's horn announces the King. It is a royal fanfare.
verses.reflect: How do you picture God's reign? How could you celebrate it today?
verses.alt: Rams' horns are raised by priests on a mountain stairway.

verses.title: Sing praises
verses.heading: A fourfold call to sing
verses.meaning: Sing praises to God, sing praises; sing praises to our King, sing praises! The command to sing appears four times in one verse. The repetition is deliberate and joyful. 'Our King' is personal: God is King of all the earth and also of His people. The verse is meant to be sung aloud. It shows that worship is not passive; it is a response called for again and again.
verses.context: Psalm 150 calls for praise thirteen times, and Psalm 96:1–2 repeats 'sing to the LORD' three times. Psalm 47:6 uses a fourfold command, twice to 'God' and twice to 'our King.'
explore: Sing praises
The command is repeated four times. Praise is urgent.
Our King
God is personal King. The community claims Him as its own.
verses.reflect: What song could you sing to God today, even if only quietly?
verses.alt: A choir of singers in linen robes stands in rows on temple steps.

verses.title: A psalm of praise
verses.heading: God King of all the earth
verses.meaning: For God is King of all the earth; sing to Him a psalm of praise. The reason for singing is repeated: God is King of all the earth. The phrase 'a psalm of praise' translates the word Maskil, which can mean a skillful or instructive song. Praise should be thoughtful as well as joyful. The verse calls for worship that understands why God is to be praised.
verses.context: The word translated 'psalm of praise' is Maskil, used in many psalm headings. 1 Corinthians 14:15 says, 'I will sing with my spirit, but I will also sing with my mind.'
explore: King of all the earth
God's reign is universal. The praise matches its scope.
Psalm of praise
Praise should be skillful. Thought and joy go together.
verses.reflect: How could you praise God with both your mind and your heart?
verses.alt: A lyre and a scroll of music lie on a sunlit window ledge.

verses.title: Seated on His holy throne
verses.heading: God reigns over the nations
verses.meaning: God reigns over the nations; God is seated on His holy throne. The verse declares God's reign in the present tense. He rules all nations and sits on a holy throne. Holiness means His rule is pure and set apart. 'Seated' pictures settled authority, not a temporary position. The vision is like Isaiah 6, where the prophet sees the Lord seated on a throne.
verses.context: Isaiah 6:1 sees the Lord seated on a high and lofty throne, and Revelation 4:2 describes a throne in heaven with One seated on it. Psalm 47:8 declares God's present reign.
explore: God reigns
The verb is present tense. God's rule is happening now, not only in the future.
Holy throne
His authority is pure. His reign is set apart from every corrupt human throne.
verses.reflect: What difference does it make that God reigns now, not only in the future?
verses.alt: An empty radiant throne stands amid clouds and light.

verses.title: People of the God of Abraham
verses.heading: Nations gathered to God
verses.meaning: The nobles of the nations have assembled as the people of the God of Abraham; for the shields of the earth belong to God; He is highly exalted. The psalm ends with a remarkable vision. Leaders of the nations gather and become the people of Abraham's God. This fulfills the promise that all nations would be blessed through Abraham (Genesis 12:3). The shields, representing rulers or defenses, belong to God. He is exalted above them all.
verses.context: Genesis 12:3 promises blessing for all families through Abraham, and Galatians 3:8 calls that promise the gospel announced in advance. Revelation 7:9 sees a multitude from every nation before the throne.
explore: The God of Abraham
Abraham's God becomes the nations' God. The promise is fulfilled.
Shields belong to God
Rulers and defenses are His. Every power is under Him.
verses.reflect: How does this vision of the nations gathered to God shape your view of people unlike you?
verses.alt: Envoys from many lands lay shields before a temple.
